StringWithMarkup.String: Demeton-S's former production and use as a component of the insecticide demeton resulted in its direct release to the environment. If released to air, a vapor pressure of 2.6X10-4 mm Hg at 25 °C indicates demeton-S will exist in both the vapor and particulate phases in the atmosphere. Vapor-phase demeton-S will be degraded in the atmosphere by reaction with photochemically-produced hydroxyl radicals; the half-life for this reaction in air is estimated to be 5 hours. Particulate-phase demeton-S will be removed from the atmosphere by wet or dry deposition. Demeton-S undergoes photolysis on soil surfaces indicating that it may be susceptible to photolysis in the atmosphere. If released to soil, demeton-S is expected to have high mobility based upon a Koc value of 70 measured in an unspecified soil. Volatilization from moist soil surfaces is not expected to be an important fate process based upon an estimated Henry's Law constant of 4.9X10-8 atm-cu m/mole. Demeton-S is not expected to volatilize from dry soil surfaces given its vapor pressure. Demeton-S was photolyzed 69, 74, and 24% when incorporated into 3 different soils and irradiated in natural sunlight for 8 days, suggesting direct or indirect photolysis may be an important fate process for this compound on soil surfaces. If released into water, demeton-S is not expected to adsorb to suspended solids and sediment based upon the Koc value. Volatilization from water surfaces is not expected to be an important fate process based upon this compound's estimated Henry's Law constant. The chemical hydrolysis half-life of demeton-S was reported as 53 days at pH 5.7 and 27 °C, with 1,2-bis(ethylthio)ethane identified as its major degradation product. An estimated BCF of 8 suggests the potential for bioconcentration in aquatic organisms is low. Since demeton is no longer registered for use in the United States, current occupational exposure and exposure to the general population is expected to be low or non-existent. (SRC)

Section.Description: Sorption to soils and sediments is an important factor on the transport and fate of organic contaminants in the environment.  The soil/water adsorption coefficient, also known as solid-water distribution coefficient (Kd), measures the amount of chemical substance adsorbed onto soil per amount of water.  Since adsorption occurs predominantly by partition into the soil organic matter, it is more useful to normalize the Kd value to the organic carbon content of a soil and express the distribution coefficient in Koc (organic carbon normalized distribution coefficient).  The greater the Kd (or Koc) value, the less likely a chemical will leach or contribute to runoff.  A very high value means it is strongly adsorbed onto soil and organic matter and does not move throughout the soil.
